title: Latvia Launches 'Namejs '26' National Defense Exercise — 12,000 Troops Including US, Canadian, Baltic Forces Under NATO Multinational Division North
detail: Latvia's National Armed Forces launched the comprehensive national defense exercise 'Namejs '26' on September 2, 2026, running through October 8 — the largest annual Baltic drill of the year. Approximately 12,000 servicemen, reservists and National Guard volunteers are participating, including units from Canada, the United States, Estonia and Lithuania, organized in cooperation with the headquarters of NATO's Multinational Division North and the NATO Force Integration Unit in Latvia. Activities include increased drone operations near border areas, military equipment and personnel movements nationwide, low-altitude aircraft flights, and live-fire exercises. The National Armed Forces are also running mobilization drills as part of Namejs '26, testing integration of Home Guard and reserve personnel into the combat structure, and working with the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) on situational awareness and collective response in the Baltic region. As with BALTOPS 26 in June, the exercise illustrates the operational-level paradox running through the NATO-US relationship in 2026: US forces continue to train and integrate under NATO's Multinational Division North even as the Pentagon's Europe force posture review — due to deliver troop-level options to Hegseth by November 6 — leaves the future scale of that American presence unresolved.

title: Denmark Deploys Conscripts to Greenland for First Time as Arctic Tensions With US Persist
detail: Denmark deployed conscripts to Greenland for the first time in recent history, Reuters reported September 2, 2026, as part of Arctic Endurance — a Danish cold-weather training exercise involving roughly 400 personnel from ten NATO countries, including Nordic home-guard units, French infantry, a Belgian drone unit, Dutch marines, and Finnish and Danish special forces. The deployment falls under Arctic Sentry, a NATO mission launched in 2026 to reinforce the alliance's Arctic presence and ease tensions within NATO stemming from President Trump's repeated demands that the US acquire Greenland on national-security grounds — demands Denmark and Greenland have both rejected. Copenhagen has committed additional funding to Arctic defense capabilities after acknowledging years of underinvestment in the region. One 19-year-old conscript said the deployment 'shows presence that we're here and not just thinking of our own skin'; Danish exercise officer Captain Laura Jepsen said the goal was 'to continue the training of the conscripts, the soldiers, and get more experience with the training in the Arctic terrain and climate.' Russia, which maintains the Arctic's largest military footprint, has criticized NATO's expanding Arctic activity as a security threat that heightens confrontation risk; China has also increased its Arctic engagement in partnership with Moscow.

media.caption: A Danish conscript trains in Greenland as part of Arctic Endurance, part of NATO's Arctic Sentry mission
